::: {.why}
A flat cost assumption in basis points is wrong by an order of magnitude across your universe, and last night's ten numbers show you in which direction.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report the quoted spread in basis points as a function of market capitalisation or dollar volume for your universe.
- Say what fraction of the quoted spread you would actually pay on a small passive order, and why it is less than half.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Fit the relationship rather than tabulating it: regress log spread on log dollar volume across your universe and report the slope. That single coefficient lets you assign a spread estimate to any name in your universe, including ones you have no quote data for.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Separate effective from quoted: the effective spread paid is typically well below the quoted spread because of price improvement and mid-point execution. Note what you cannot measure without trade data, and state the assumption your cost model will make in the meantime, with its direction of error.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Add the fitted spread function to a new qlib/costs.py, taking a symbol and a date and returning an estimated half-spread in basis points.
:::
:::

## Deliverable

::: {.deliverable}
qlib/costs.py with a fitted spread-versus-liquidity function, and the regression slope reported.
:::

## Checkpoint

::: {.checkpoint}
Your spread model says 3 basis points for SPY and 45 for a small cap. What produced that ratio, and what does it do to a strategy that trades both?
:::
